Dengue Fever Knows No Season, So Mosquito Swarms Never Stop Eradicating Larvae 
 KESEHATAN LINGKUNGAN Dengue Fever Knows No Season, So Mosquito Swarms Never Stop Eradicating Larvae
 Mosquito larvae are no longer confined to the rainy season; their presence is now evident year-round. Jumantik has become the frontline force in combating them.
 16 Nov 2026 07:00 WIB · Kesehatan 
 Santi Ariani
 Kecil Sedang Besar Sangat Besar Share
 Copy Link
 By Ni Wayan Santi Ariani 
 This article has been translated using AI. See original . 
 00:00 00:00 10 10 1.00x Moments after the rain falls, it leaves behind not just the scent of wet earth and a chill in the air. Puddles in various road depressions, plant pots, and even unexpected places serve as reminders that rain has passed through the area.
 The resulting puddles have the potential to become a breeding ground for mosquito larvae. However, this doesn't mean that other seasons will be free from dengue-carrying mosquitoes (Aedes aegypti).
 In reality, mosquito larvae continue to be found regardless of the season, the threat of dengue fever remains a concern, and mosquito larvae monitors must persist in their efforts to eliminate these larvae.
 Today, Friday (13/11/2026) at 8:30 AM WIB, dozens of women gathered in front of the Hankam Multipurpose Building in Slipi, West Jakarta. They are jumantik cadres from each neighborhood unit in RW 002 of Palmerah sub-district, who will carry out a mosquito nest eradication (PSN) activity in residents' homes.
 Equipped with forms, pens, and flashlights, the jumantik navigated through main roads and narrow alleys to reach residents' homes. They were divided into two groups, with each group responsible for visiting and inspecting approximately 15 households.
 Throughout the visit, laughter frequently echoed among the jumantik. The community clean-up activities resembled a relaxed family gathering, yet adhered to established procedures. In addition to checking for mosquito larvae, educational messages and reminders about vigilance were often shared during the event.
 This is because, although sources of stagnant water often appear during the rainy season, it is still possible to find mosquito larvae during the dry season. Therefore, weekly visits and inspections of every household have become mandatory activities for the mosquito monitors.
 During today's PSN operation, out of a total of 35 homes visited, three were found to have mosquito larvae.
 The person in charge of the Environmental Health Program at the Palmerah Community Health Center, Muhammad Agus Setiawan, reported that mosquito larvae are commonly found in potted plants and discarded items in residents' yards.
 "Because at home, people are reminded to empty the bathtub and many people use buckets," he said.
 Agus explained that the findings were promptly addressed by the mosquito monitors. Residents were also reminded to remain vigilant about the growth of mosquito larvae outside their homes.
 "We immediately disposed of the larvae, and we also educated residents to be more careful," he said.
 In addition to PSN activities, mosquito larvae checks are also routinely conducted independently by each jumantik at least twice a week. One such check was carried out by Nurhikmah (48), a resident of RT 002 RW 004 in the Kemanggisan neighborhood of Palmerah, West Jakarta.
 Every Wednesday and Friday, he will conduct visits and inspections at residents' homes, with hidden places being the most concerning.
 "Sometimes we see that there are mosquito larvae in houses, and that's the main thing we look for. Usually, mosquito larvae are found in open bathroom sinks, gaps in dispensers, and plant pot stands," he said.
 To that end, he must always be diligent in inspecting the puddles in each resident's home, even though he often encounters obstacles along the way.
 During his visits, he sometimes encounters empty houses or buildings where the occupants are not present. On the other hand, there are also residents who are reluctant to have their homes visited and inspected.
 "Sometimes there are residents who refuse our visits, usually those who have just moved in, so it's more challenging; we have to explain things to them first," he said.
 In another area, Afifah Maulidina, commonly known as Dina (27), a resident of RT 010 RW 005 in North Grogol, South Jakarta, also makes weekly visits to residents' homes. As a jumantik cadre, Dina is responsible for monitoring the presence of mosquito larvae in over 50 households. She typically conducts these activities twice a week, on Wednesdays and Thursdays.
 During each inspection of residents' homes, he must repeatedly remind them about mosquito larvae and take immediate action to eliminate any larvae he finds. This is crucial, given the rapid breeding and growth of mosquito larvae in the area.
 "We go inside and if there are larvae, we throw away the water or fill it with abate powder to prevent them from growing again. Because if we leave the water uncovered for just three days, usually there will be larvae," he said.
 In her neighborhood, Dina found the most mosquito larvae growing in residents' bathtubs. Therefore, this became one of the most important things to pay attention to during inspections. "People with large ceramic bathtubs often rarely empty them because once they fill it, it immediately fills up," she said.
 In addition, the drainage areas around residential neighborhoods or buildings were also subject to inspection. Dina noted that the outdoor spaces of homes, which can collect stagnant water, often serve as comfortable breeding grounds for mosquitoes.
 "Outside the house, there could be mosquito larvae every day, especially if there are neglected buckets or water containers at school," he said.
 The jumantik activities continue to be carried out regularly, regardless of the rainy season, due to the persistent potential for mosquito larvae. In instances where confirmed cases of dengue fever arise, inspections and jumantik efforts become even more intensified.
 "We are extremely vigilant when conducting home surveys, especially if someone has contracted dengue fever. We fear it could spread in our own area, so we strive to enhance our accuracy," he stated.
 Reaching out to the community
 The presence of jumantik in every neighborhood association (RT) and community unit (RW) should serve as an extension of the community health center to reach the public. The complexity of urban residents, high mobility, and the year-round breeding of mosquito larvae underscore the increasing necessity for the role of jumantik.
 "Their role is crucial, not just for us but for many others as well. It's hard to imagine what it would be like without the jumantik, as we would have to conduct the monitoring ourselves," said Ajie Trisna Hartadi, the Environmental Health Program Coordinator at the Palmerah Community Health Center, during an interview on Thursday (12/11/2026).
 Ajie emphasized the critical role of jumantik, stating that training for each cadre is conducted to the fullest extent possible. Before taking on their duties as jumantik, cadres typically receive two types of training.
 First, specialized training is conducted twice a year. Cadres are typically gathered in the community health center hall to refresh their knowledge on various aspects.
 This includes information about mosquitoes that cause dengue fever, dengue fever transmission, epidemiological investigations, and case management.
 Secondly, weekly training is conducted every Friday immediately following the mosquito nest eradication (PSN) activities. Typically, the community health center will hold a discussion session that includes an evaluation of the performance of Jumantik cadres.
 The vanguard of prevention
 Young entomologist from the DKI Jakarta Provincial Health Office, Aan Aryanti, stated that the rise in dengue fever is often linked to climate change. Increased humidity affects the survival and breeding capacity of mosquitoes.
 "The rainy season creates natural breeding grounds, such as in trees and other inaccessible areas," he said during an interview on Thursday (12/11/2026).
 However, data on dengue fever cases in Jakarta reveals a slightly different picture. It was explained that as the climate changes, dengue cases persist, albeit with fluctuating numbers.
 "Every year, there are always reports of dengue fever. Even though the climate changes, cases remain, never zero or very low," he said.
 Meanwhile, from January to November 9, 2026, 8,058 cases of dengue infection were recorded in Jakarta. This figure includes all manifestations of dengue, namely dengue hemorrhagic fever (DHF), dengue fever (DF), and dengue shock syndrome (DSS).
 The figure has reportedly decreased compared to 2025, which recorded 9,431 dengue fever cases. Despite the decline in the number of cases, the fluctuating rates of dengue fever still underscore the need for preventive measures.
 Aan stated that jumantik serve as the frontline in preventing and controlling the risk of dengue fever in the community. Currently, there are over 32,000 jumantik cadres registered in neighborhood associations (RT and RW) across Jakarta.
 "The more residents who become mosquito larvae monitors, the better the environment will be," he said.
